events.text: The entrance trial of {b3_order} is held in the yard behind the rice mill. A line of hopefuls stands in the cold, each holding a wooden staff. The examiner, a broad woman with flour on her sleeves, walks the line and says one thing to each. To you she says: 'Hold it as if you were not afraid of dropping it.'

effects.log: You hold it loosely and, to your surprise, it settles in your hands like a cat. The examiner grunts and moves on. It is her whole review, and it is enough.
You grip it hard, and your knuckles whiten. She stops, pries one finger open, and says, kindly, 'Again.' You do it again.

events.text: The trial of {b3_order} asks each hopeful to carry two buckets of water up the hill road, without spilling, and to say something kind to whoever they meet on the way. A goat-herd and a tax clerk are on the road. The goat-herd only wants to be left alone. The clerk is crying over a ledger.

effects.log: You put down the buckets, listen to the clerk's trouble for ten minutes, and arrive late with half a bucket. The examiner marks you high for the clerk, and low for the water.

choices.text: Say good morning and hurry on

effects.log: You say good morning to both, and arrive with full buckets. The examiner marks you adequate. The clerk, behind you, is still crying.

events.text: At the trial of {b3_order} the examiners set a puzzle, not a fight. A wooden box, a locked door, and a string. You have the string. Behind you a dozen hopefuls are trying to break the door down. An old man in the corner, who is also an examiner, is eating an apple and watching your hands.

effects.log: You pull the string. The door, which was never locked, swings open. The old examiner nods, finishes his apple, and writes a single word: 'Looked.'

choices.text: Join the others at the door

effects.log: You push with the others. The door holds. The old man chews, shakes his head sadly, and writes a different word, which is 'Pushed.'

events.text: Before the trial begins, the head of {b3_order} asks every hopeful to name the person they most want to protect. The answers are quiet, and mostly mothers. One boy says his dog. A girl says she doesn't know, and starts to cry. The head writes each one down and says: 'Good. Now we know what you will fight for.'

effects.log: You name them. The head writes it down in a small neat hand. Years later the page is found, and read aloud at your wedding or your funeral, whichever comes first.

choices.text: Say you do not know yet

effects.log: The head writes: 'Open.' They look at you a long moment. 'That is a fine answer,' they say. 'It is the only honest one.' You pass.

events.text: The trial of {b3_order} ends with a bout against a senior pupil, who has been told to lose if you show courage and to win if you do not. The senior is a tall, nervous young person with a split lip. They bow. They have clearly never been told how to do this part.

effects.log: You fight your best. The senior, relieved, fights theirs. You lose by a hair, and the examiners, nodding, give you a place.
You watch, and they watch you. It is a dull bout. But you notice their hands tremble, and you stop, and tell them it is fine. The examiners mark that down, warmly.

events.text: The examiner at {b3_order} asks you to stand in the yard, in the rain, for an hour, and do nothing. It is the whole of the trial. Others around you are fidgeting. One boy has started to hum. A girl is being sick behind a barrel. The rain runs down your collar.

effects.log: You stand, and it is a long, wet, honest hour. At the end, the examiner hands you a dry cloth and says nothing. It is the best welcome you ever get.
You hum, low, in a harmony. By the end of the hour half the yard is humming. The examiner pretends to scowl, and fails, and writes a long note.

events.text: The trial of {b3_order} requires a hopeful to bring a gift for the school. The gifts pile up at the gate: a pot of honey, a sharp new knife, a book of songs. You have brought a loaf you baked yourself, a little burnt. A porter takes it with an impassive face, and puts it at the bottom of the pile.

effects.log: You ask. The porter hands it over with obvious relief. You eat it on the road, burnt, and are fine. You are told later it was the only gift the school did not have to pay to store.
You leave it. That night, in the school kitchen, the head of the school breaks bread with the cooks and finds the burnt loaf. The head eats it, all of it, and pronounces it 'honest.'

events.text: The examiners of {b3_order} have a custom: they send a stranger to ask each hopeful for help. Yours is a little girl with a lost coin and a worried face. You have a full day of trial before you, and a long list of things to prove. She asks if you can look under the cart.

effects.log: You find the coin, and some dirt, and a very surprised cat. The girl beams. Later you learn she was the head's niece, and the cat was bribed.

choices.text: Tell her you cannot, you are busy

effects.log: She nods and goes. The trial goes well. The head, hearing of it, says only: 'Good.' It is not clear which part.

events.text: Your trial at {b3_order} is to defend a flag for an hour, in a circle drawn in chalk, against any who come. The flag is plain cloth. The attackers are boys of the school, instructed to try. One, a short broad one, grins at you. You can tell he has been enjoying this for years.

effects.log: You hold the circle till the hour is out. The short boy is panting, delighted, and shakes your hand. 'You are a wall,' he says. You are a wall for a living, afterwards.
You hold it out. He stops, stunned. 'Nobody has ever done that,' he says. He takes it, and then hands it back. The examiners are not sure what to write.

events.text: At the end of the trial the examiners of {b3_order} serve every hopeful a bowl of plain soup, and watch who shares and who hoards. You have taken yours. Beside you a small, hungry-looking boy is staring at the bowl he has not been given, because the kitchen ran out. He is not complaining.

effects.log: You pour half of it into his cup. He drinks it with great care. You are told afterward that this was the real trial, and that you passed, thin and hungry.

choices.text: Ask the cook for another bowl

effects.log: The cook, caught, produces a pot from nowhere. The boy gets his soup. The trial is passed by many, and the cook is told off by the head, with a barely hidden smile.

events.text: {b3_order} sends you up the river road with a basket of seed-cakes and a letter, to a village that has not paid its dues in three years. You are not to ask for the money. You are to be pleasant. The village has one tavern, one temple, and one very large, very old dog on the bridge who will not let you pass.

effects.log: The dog eats the cake, sighs, and rolls over. The village, which has been watching from windows, comes out to see who tamed it. The dues arrive within the week, in a pot.
You wade the ford, soaked to the knee, and arrive late. The village feeds you, and complains of the dog. You leave with a good meal and nothing else.

events.text: An errand for {b3_order}: deliver a sack of dried fish to a widow at the end of a mountain road. She is the mother of a pupil who left. The pupil sent no word. You carry the fish and a letter you have not been told the contents of. The widow opens the door before you knock. She has seen you coming for an hour.

choices.text: Hand over the fish and the letter

effects.log: She reads it standing. She does not cry. She asks you to sit, and gives you tea, and says her son always was bad at writing. You stay the night.

choices.text: Tell her what you know of her son

effects.log: You tell her he is well, and thin, and funny. It is mostly true. She nods, and tucks a rice-ball in your pocket, and says: 'You are a good liar. Thank you.'

events.text: For {b3_order} you are sent to settle a dispute between two neighbouring farms over a stray cow. The cow is in the middle of the road, chewing. Both farmers are shouting. Each has a cord around the cow's neck, and each is certain it is theirs. The cow has a bell with a name on it, in letters you cannot read.

effects.log: You speak to the cow, softly. It walks to the left, to the farm with the lower fence, and goes in the gate. Both farmers fall silent. The one who is right is the one with the lower fence. He gives you a cheese.
A passing priest reads the bell. It says 'Daisy, belonging to the miller.' Neither farmer has a mill. The miller turns up, red and apologetic. You are paid for the afternoon.

events.text: {b3_order} sends you to guard a wedding procession over a bad stretch of road. The bride is a farmer's daughter, the groom a ferryman, and the procession is mostly goats. The road runs between two hills where bandits have lately been seen. The bride walks with her chin up, humming a tune. The goats are not.

effects.log: You walk beside her, hand on your staff. No bandits come. At the end she gives you a ribbon, and the groom a nod, and you are fed enormously at the feast and remembered for years.
You scout the hills and meet two bandits, who are, you discover, the groom's cousins, there to stand guard. You all walk down together, cheerfully, and are late to the wedding.

events.text: A year of errands for {b3_order}: you carry a message to a distant temple, bring a child home from the wrong side of the river, collect a debt of eleven coppers, and mend a bridge. The bridge is a plank. The child is furious. The temple monk gives you tea and asks if you have seen the Maker lately. You say you have not.

effects.log: He says everyone has, and nobody knows. He talks for an hour, gently, about a thing that happens at the edge of sleep. You leave a little puzzled, and warmed.
He smiles, and presses a small clay figure into your hand. It is a lopsided bird. You carry it for the rest of the journey and put it on your windowsill.

events.text: You are sent by {b3_order} to buy a hundred candles for the winter, and the chandler wants twice the usual price. He is not a cheat: the wax is dear this year. He looks at you with a tired, honest face. A cheaper chandler, three villages over, is rumoured to be dishonest. You have two days.

effects.log: You pay it, and bring the school a bundle of expensive, slow-burning candles. The head says nothing about the price, and burns one every night, for you, in the kitchen.
The cheaper chandler is honest, as it turns out, and brisk. You save twelve coins and a day, and the first chandler, hearing, sends you a thoughtful letter.

events.text: An errand takes you to the market town, where {b3_order} has a stall selling bandages and tea. The stall is run by a retired pupil who is nearly blind and sharper than anyone. They know your step on the stones before you speak. They ask for news, and a coin, and a story, in that order.

effects.log: You give all three. The old pupil tells you a story in return, about the school's first head, which you will tell for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Give a story, keep the coin

effects.log: You give them the story. They laugh, and say it's worth a coin, and give you one, from the till. You leave a little richer.

events.text: {b3_order} gives you a sealed jar to carry to a hermit on the hill. It is heavy and hums. You are told not to open it, and not to drop it, and not to let it get wet. It rains, naturally. You shelter in a goatherd's shed, with the jar on your knees, and the goatherd's daughter peers at it.

choices.text: Show her it through the crack

effects.log: The jar contains a small, very bright, very annoyed beetle. The girl is delighted. The hermit, later, says the beetle's temper was a test of the carrier's. You passed.
The jar stays dry and unseen. The hermit receives it with a bow. In return he gives you a paper packet of tea, which is, you find, the best in the district.

events.text: You have been sent by {b3_order} with a message for the head of a rival school across the valley, which is on bad terms with yours over a spring. The message is a polite proposal for a feast. The rival head, a thin old man who sells herbs, reads it twice, folds it neatly, and says he will think. He does not offer you tea.

effects.log: You wait on his step for three days. On the third he comes out with a pot of tea. 'You are the first who has waited,' he says. He sends a feast invitation back with you.
You return in a week. The old man is relieved. 'I wanted to see if you would come back,' he says. The feast is held, and the spring is shared on alternate days.

events.text: The cart-road to the next kingdom has washed out, and {b3_order} sends you to help clear it. The work is mud and rope and shouting. A merchant is stranded on the far side with a cart of pottery, wringing his hat. A donkey stands in the middle of the flood and looks at everyone with a calm contempt.

choices.text: Carry the pottery over by hand

effects.log: You carry the pots across in a long, wet chain. Two break. The merchant, delighted by the rest, gives you a small blue cup. It is the nicest thing you own.
You lead the donkey out, with a carrot and a song. The cart follows. The merchant is weeping with relief. He gives you a coin and the donkey's name.

events.text: {b3_order} has you take a stone-mason's apprentice to the capital of the kingdom for his first look at the sea. He is nine, silent, and terrified of cobbles. You walk for six days. On the fifth he says his first sentence: 'Is the sea wet all the way down?' You tell him yes. He looks at you with grave respect.

effects.log: You show him the sea. He stands at the edge for an hour. At the end he picks up a stone and puts it in his pocket. 'For later,' he says. He is not a silent child again.

choices.text: Take him to the harbour market

effects.log: The harbour market is a wonder. He is given a fig by a sailor, and a bird by a woman, and a story by an old man with one eye. You walk him home laden, and he sleeps in the cart.

events.text: The errand from {b3_order} is to find a lost bell. It was a small brass one, hung over the school gate, and a gust took it in the night. The head wants it back by the full moon. The valley is large and the bell small. A schoolboy tells you he saw a crow with something shiny in its beak, heading east.

effects.log: You follow the crow to a ruined tower, where a nest is lined with bright things. Your bell is in it, between a spoon and a button. You climb up, and are pecked, and succeed.
You ask in six villages. The seventh has it: an old woman hung it on her goat, who likes the sound. She sells it back for a bun. The goat looks wounded.

events.text: You are sent by {b3_order} to collect a debt from a miller, who cannot pay. He has a sick wife, a leaking roof, and a daughter who does not look up from her sewing. He offers you what he has: a sack of flour and an apology. You have been told to come back with coin.

choices.text: Take the flour and forgive the rest

effects.log: You take the flour, and say the school will wait. The miller weeps. The head, told, is quiet, and then adds, 'Good,' and writes off the rest.
You press. The miller finds seven coins in a boot and gives them with shame. You carry them home heavy, and the head, taking them, says: 'That was not worth the miller's face.'

events.text: {b3_order} sends you to help with the autumn harvest in a village that has promised the school a tenth of its rice. The work is hard and bright. In the evening you eat with the family, and the eldest son, a cheerful lad with a bandaged hand, asks you shyly to teach him a throw. He has always wanted to learn.

effects.log: You teach him a simple one. He practises it on a sack of rice all night. By the end of the week he can do it, and is the village's pride. His mother sends you off with two chickens.
You work the fields and rest. You come home with a back like a drum, and a bag of rice, and a quiet gratitude that is its own reward.

events.text: On an errand for {b3_order} you are caught in a storm and sheltered in a cottage by a woman with a bright hearth and a cat on every chair. She is nearly deaf. She asks you, three times, who you are. Each time you tell her. At last she says, 'Ah, the Maker's own,' and gives you a blanket.

effects.log: 'It's what I say to everyone,' she says. 'It makes them stand up straighter.' You laugh. In the morning you do stand a little straighter, all the way home.
You sleep in the warm, under a pile of cats. In the morning she has mended your cloak, and says nothing about it. You leave a coin on the table, and she leaves it there.

events.text: The library of {b3_order} is a long low room above the stables, and smells of straw and ink. The librarian, a stooped young man with a cough, hands you a lamp and says the third shelf is not to be touched. It is the third shelf that you are here for. He turns his back, studiously, and coughs.

effects.log: You take the scroll, and copy it by lamp, and put it back. The librarian turns round, finds nothing missing, and says, 'Good.' He coughs again, with relief.
He sighs, and gives you the scroll himself, with a warning, and a cup of barley water. He is a better friend after that than he was a clerk.

events.text: In the cellar of {b3_order} there is a chest nobody has opened since the first head died. The key hangs on a nail beside it, in plain sight, with a note: 'Not yet.' The chest is plain, bound in iron. A small mouse has made a nest on top. You are told you may have an hour in the cellar.

effects.log: You sit with the mouse and the chest for an hour, and say a prayer to the Maker for the one who is buried in the school's memory. When you rise, the mouse is asleep on your shoe.
The key turns. Inside is a folded cloth, a sword-belt and a letter that says: 'You were told not yet.' You close the chest. The mouse looks at you, unimpressed.

events.text: The treasury of {b3_order} is a locked cupboard with a very good lock. It holds the school's gold: eleven coins and a button. The head lets you count it. 'It's the most honest treasury in the kingdom,' they say. It is. The button is made of jade.

effects.log: You count: eleven coins, one button. You report both. The head nods. 'Now you know what we have. Now you know what we need.' You get a small raise in trust.

choices.text: Quietly add a coin of your own

effects.log: You add a coin. The head counts later and finds twelve, and smiles, and says nothing. The button is polished, that week, for no reason you can name.

events.text: Among the dusty scrolls of {b3_order} you find a diary written by a pupil two hundred years ago. It is full of complaints about the food, and the head, and the weather. It is, you realise, entirely about you. The pupil has the same fears, the same jokes, the same dislike of cabbage. The last page says: 'If you read this, hello.'

choices.text: Write a reply on the last page

effects.log: You write: 'Hello. It is still cabbage.' You add the date. The diary goes back on the shelf. In some distant year another pupil will read both, and understand.
It takes two nights. By the end you have a strange friendship with a long-dead stranger. You stand a little taller, knowing you are not the first to hate cabbage.

events.text: The school's training manual, a thick book bound in goatskin, has a missing page. Everyone knows it, and nobody mentions it. This week an old pupil comes by, ninety if a day, and says she has the page, in her head, and will tell it to whoever asks properly. She is sitting in the sun with a cup of tea.

effects.log: You bow, and ask. She tells it in her cracked voice, a sequence of seven movements. Her eyes go bright. You write it down. She gives you the rest of her tea.

choices.text: Ask her for the story behind it

effects.log: She tells you the story, a long, sad, funny one about the pupil who tore out the page. You don't ask for the movements. She tells you them anyway, as a thank-you.

events.text: A hidden room behind the library of {b3_order} contains a case of old weapons: a bent spear, a blunt dagger, a sword with a chip. Each has a label, in the school's first head's hand, saying what it was used for. The labels are the strangest part. 'This one, to cut bread.' 'This one, to open a letter.' 'This one, to say sorry.'

effects.log: You read all forty. Each has a small, human use. At the end you understand why the school has never killed anyone, and why it is so proud of it.

choices.text: Take the sword that says sorry

effects.log: You take it, and use it, once, to say sorry to someone you wronged. It works. You put it back with a new label in your own hand.

events.text: There is a chest of letters in the cellar of {b3_order}, from former pupils, written over the years and never sent. They were meant for the head, and never delivered. The head has asked you to burn them. They are all in different hands. You read the top one, by accident. It says: 'I'm sorry I left.'

effects.log: You burn them in the stove, one by one. The smoke goes up, thin, sweet. The head, watching from the door, says: 'Thank you.' You have not told anyone what the top one said.
You read them, one by one, and learn more about the school than any head could. You burn them last, in a ring of salt. You carry every one of them, quietly, for the rest of your life.

events.text: The vault of {b3_order} is guarded by a goose. It is a very old goose, bad-tempered and honest. It will let in the pupils it likes and hiss at the ones it doesn't. It has hissed at you every day for a week. This morning, for no reason, it looks at you with its head tilted, and steps aside.

effects.log: You go in, and bow. The goose honks once, approvingly. The vault is dusty and quiet, and you find nothing you were told to look for, and a great deal you were not.
The goose eats it, slowly. Then it sits on your foot, and will not move. You are told you now have a goose. You do.

events.text: To spy on {b3_foe} you take work in their kitchen. It is easier than you expected: no one asks questions of a woman with a ladle. The cook is a large, kind man who calls you 'little dumpling' and slips you a bun when no one is looking. You learn the school's secrets by smell and gossip. He is the nicest enemy you have met.

choices.text: Take what you came for and go

effects.log: You carry your report back to {b3_order}, and the cook's bun, wrapped in cloth, in your pocket. You eat it on the road. You cannot taste it.

choices.text: Stay another season with the cook

effects.log: You stay another season. You learn nothing new and cook a great deal. When you leave he gives you a recipe, and you give him none of the school's secrets. Both of you win.

events.text: Inside {b3_foe} you are given a bed in the loft and a cloak that is a little too big. At night you hear one of the pupils, a boy of twelve, weeping into his sleeve. He is homesick. He has not told anyone. You are meant to be learning the school's training schedule, and the boy is making enough noise to wake the roof.

effects.log: You sit by him, and say nothing, and then tell him about the town you grew up in. He sleeps. You lie awake and are not at all sure which of you is the spy.
You lie quietly, and learn their drill, their watches and the hour the gate is barred. You carry it back, and it is useful, and you think of the boy for years.

events.text: The head of {b3_foe} has asked you to carry a message to a tavern, in code, to a man in a green coat. It is a test. You know it is. You suspect they know you know. The message is a folded piece of paper with a drawing of a fish. The man in the green coat is waiting by the stove, whittling.

effects.log: The man in the green coat takes the paper, grunts, and gives you a drink. The fish was a joke between the head and the man. You are in. You are, apparently, also funny.
You unfold it. It says: 'Do not read this.' You fold it again. The man takes it with a nod. The head, afterward, says: 'I knew you would.' You are not sure if it is praise.

events.text: A pupil of {b3_foe} has become your friend, and invites you to their mother's house for the festival. It is a lovely house, with a lemon tree and a dog. The mother makes dumplings. You are, you remember, here to find out where the school keeps its stores. The dumplings are excellent.

effects.log: You eat eleven dumplings and sing a song after. You learn nothing of use. The friend, years later, will be the one who saves your life.
The friend, easily, tells you. You carry it back with a stone in your stomach. The friend never learns. You never go to that house again, and think of the lemon tree often.

events.text: The rival school {b3_foe} has a hidden courtyard where they train their best, and you have been told to find it. You search for days. At last you hear it: the rhythm of a drum, and shouted counts, behind a wall of ivy. You climb a tree. You see a dozen pupils performing a drill so beautiful that you forget to take notes.

effects.log: You watch till dusk. You fall out of the tree. They catch you, politely, and give you a cup of water and a seat, and let you go. 'Tell your head we say hello,' they say.
You take careful notes, and slip away at the end. Back at the school you draw the drill from memory. It is the best work of your life and you cannot say who taught it to you.

events.text: A rumour inside {b3_foe} says there is a spy among them, and they are quietly checking every pupil's hands for calluses from the wrong school. Yours are right, but a little too neat. The head is going from bed to bed with a lamp. You are third in the row. You can hear the lamp coming.

choices.text: Roughen your hands with a rock

effects.log: You rub your palms on a brick. The head arrives, looks, nods. The next bed's pupil, a child, is whisked out for questioning. You have the sick sense of having bought your safety with a child's.
You sit up and say who you are. The head, tired, nods. 'We knew,' they say. 'We wanted to see if you would stay.' You are sent home with a loaf and a warning.

events.text: In the loft of {b3_foe} you overhear a conversation between two seniors about a plan: to ambush your school's team at the spring festival. They speak in a low, tight, cheerful way. You have the whole plan before you. One of them, whom you like, is laughing at her own joke. You could stop it, or you could stay hidden.

effects.log: You carry the warning home. The ambush is foiled, with nobody hurt. The senior you liked is punished, and later sends you an unforgiving letter. It stays with you.
You take the seniors aside and say: it's a bad plan. They, stunned, drop it. Your cover is gone, but the festival goes ahead in peace, and you are not thanked.

events.text: The kitchen of {b3_foe} serves you a bowl of soup the day you are to leave, and the cook, a great fat fellow, slides a note under it. It says: 'I know who you are. I like you. Go home, little dumpling, and be careful.' You eat the soup, and fold the note into your sleeve. Your eyes are stinging.

effects.log: You thank him on the way out. He waves a ladle and looks at the ceiling. You carry the note for twenty years, and it is among the three things in your trunk you would save.
You say nothing and leave. At the gate you are given a package. It contains a bun. You eat it on the road.

events.text: The first morning as head of {b3_order} you find that the old head, {b3_oldhead}, has left a note on your desk, in a scrawl: 'The roof leaks over the east bed. The cat is called Biscuit. Don't let the cook near the flour sacks.' That is the whole of the handover. You sit down and read it three times.

effects.log: You mend the roof. It takes a week and three ladders. The east bed's pupil is sleepier, and drier, and thanks you with a muffled, grateful snore.
Biscuit, a vast orange tom, looks you over with contempt and gets on your lap. The school, passing, decides at once that you will do.

events.text: As the new head of {b3_order} you are asked to give the opening speech to the pupils. You have written three versions. The first is grand, the second is funny, the third is a list of rules. The pupils sit in rows, shining. {b3_oldhead} sits at the back with arms folded, and gives you a small, encouraging scowl.

effects.log: You say eleven words, and sit down. The pupils, who expected an hour, are charmed. {b3_oldhead} nods once, slowly, and later says it was the best speech they have ever given.
You give the funny one. The pupils howl. {b3_oldhead} laughs so hard they drop their tea. The school adopts the funniest line as its motto.

events.text: The seat of {b3_order} comes with a ring of keys and a cupboard of unpaid bills. The bills are polite. The most pressing is a baker's, for flour, long overdue. The baker is a gentle man with a bad leg. He comes to your door with a smile and a dust of flour on his sleeve and says, 'No rush at all.'

effects.log: You pay him from the school's last coins. He is moved. For a year, a free loaf appears on your doorstep each Sunday, and is never mentioned.

choices.text: Ask for time and promise a lesson

effects.log: You promise to teach his boy a few moves. He accepts, delighted. The boy grows into the school's best baker-fighter, and the debt is paid in bread.

events.text: In your first week as head of {b3_order}, a quarrel breaks out over the use of the training yard. The younger pupils want mornings, the older want afternoons, and the cook wants the yard for drying onions. You are asked to rule. Everyone watches. A goat wanders in, unobserved, and begins to eat the onions.

effects.log: You rule that the yard belongs to whoever brings a goat. There is a stunned silence, then laughter, then a rota. The onions are saved by a very fat child with a broom.
You divide the day. Mornings, afternoons, onions. Everyone grumbles and nobody is satisfied, which is, an old pupil whispers, the mark of a fair ruling.

events.text: {b3_oldhead} leaves the school for good, on a mule, with a small bundle and a big hat. They will not say where they are going. At the gate they turn and say: 'I have always wanted to see the sea.' They ride off, humming. The pupils watch them go, and then, slowly, turn to look at you.

choices.text: Wave until they are out of sight

effects.log: You wave. You wave for a long time. Then you turn, and the pupils are waving too, in a ragged line, and the yard is very bright with the morning.

choices.text: Run after them with a flask

effects.log: You run a mile with a flask of tea. {b3_oldhead} accepts it, laughing, and says: 'There, now you are a real head.' You walk home slowly, in the sun.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have fallen out over who should lead the morning drill. Both arrive early, both stand in the middle of the yard, and both begin to call the counts. The pupils, caught between, try to follow both and tie their legs in knots. The cook, from the doorway, offers a bun to whoever will stop.

choices.text: Take one drill each, alternate days

effects.log: You set the rota. They glare at each other across the yard on alternate mornings, and the pupils, you notice, have begun to cheer for both.

choices.text: Lead it yourself for a week

effects.log: You lead it yourself. The pupils, relieved, move as one. The two seniors watch, sulking, and by the end of the week both have asked for lessons.

events.text: {b3_elder} accuses {b3_peer} of letting a rain-leak go uncorrected in the dormitory. {b3_peer} says it was {b3_elder}'s job. Both are shouting, in the corridor, over a bucket. The bucket is full. Someone has to carry it out. Both are standing very still, in the manner of two cats who both want the same hearth.

effects.log: You carry it out. The two stare at each other, and at you, with horror. By morning the roof is mended, by both of them, in silence, and nobody mentions the bucket again.

choices.text: Rule it is both their jobs

effects.log: You rule it the joint task of both. They grumble, and fix it together, and by the end are laughing about the drip.

events.text: {b3_peer} has taught the juniors a new form without asking {b3_elder}, who has taught the old form for thirty years. The juniors now perform both, depending on who is watching, which is a feat of confusion. {b3_elder} is very quiet. {b3_peer} is very pleased with themselves. The two stand on either side of the practice floor.

effects.log: You have the juniors perform both. The new form is stronger and the old is cleaner. You rule that each has a place. The two seniors stare at the floor, both secretly relieved.
You back the old form. {b3_peer} bows, stiffly, and keeps the new one alive in a corner. In five years it is the school's favourite.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} each claim that the school's sacred chestnut tree is theirs to prune. It is very old and badly overgrown. Each has a saw. They are standing at opposite ends of the tree, glaring. The pupils have formed a nervous circle. The chestnut, you note, has been dropping nuts on both of them.

effects.log: You hand them one saw between the two. They work in awkward rhythm. The tree is pruned, and thanks them with a barrage of nuts. They share a bag of them in silence.
You rule that the tree prunes itself. Both are offended. In a storm that autumn a branch falls, and fixes the argument for good.

events.text: A pupil complains that {b3_elder} is too gentle and {b3_peer} too strict, and that the school needs a mixture. Both seniors overhear. Both are stung, in opposite ways. They stand in the doorway of the training-hall, red-faced, each with a hand on the frame, and ask you whether the pupil is right.

effects.log: You say so. They are stunned. Within a month {b3_elder} has toughened, {b3_peer} has softened, and the school is calmer, and both of them, privately, are proud.

choices.text: Say both of them are right

effects.log: You say it kindly. They blink, then smile, then argue. The pupil, ashamed, is given a week of kitchen duty and a hot bun.

events.text: The school's cook says {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have been stealing biscuits from the pantry, each blaming the other. The truth is, it is both of them, on alternate nights, at about two. They have never run into each other, owing to a remarkable stroke of bad timing. You catch them both, one night, with the same biscuit.

effects.log: You take a biscuit. The three of you eat in a stunned silence by the jar. By morning a pact of the biscuit has formed, and the pantry is, in effect, theirs.
You report them. The cook, appalled and delighted, puts a lock on the biscuits. The two seniors, thereafter, are forced to share the key.

events.text: {b3_elder} has asked for leave to visit a sick friend, and {b3_peer} has said no. They are both very upright and calm, which is how you know it is serious. The sick friend is a mutual acquaintance, an old healer, whose illness is no secret. The question of who should go is, nobody will say, secretly about both of them wanting to.

effects.log: You send both, in one cart, with a hamper. They arrive and the old healer is so pleased to see them together that the fever breaks. They come home on the best of terms and the worst of tempers.

choices.text: Send one and visit the other yourself

effects.log: You send {b3_elder} and go the next week. The healer, between the two visits, has had two new stories. The healer is the winner.

events.text: A travelling merchant offers {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} each a separate bargain on a training dummy. Each has accepted. They now each own the same dummy. The merchant has left town. The dummy, a man-shaped log, stands in the yard, facing both. They have asked you to decide whose it is.

effects.log: You cut it in half. They each take a half. The two halves become mismatched training dummies, one tall and one short, and the pupils name them after the pair.
You rule it the school's. They each grumble and ask for a refund. The merchant, found weeks later in another town, refunds neither. The school gains a dummy.

events.text: {b3_peer} has started a rumour that {b3_elder} cheats at draughts. {b3_elder} has retaliated with a rumour that {b3_peer} cannot read. The rumours circulate the school, quickly, in the dark. Both are false, and the pupils love them, and have written a song. The song has seven verses. It is catchy.

effects.log: You ban the song. It is sung in whispers for a year. Both seniors confess, separately, to their rumours, and the song is un-banned and sung with pride.

choices.text: Teach the song to both of them

effects.log: You teach it to both. They sing it together, off-key. The pupils are speechless. The rumours die of embarrassment.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} were once, long ago, the closest of friends, which is why they hate each other now. The quarrel is old and tired. It has no cause left but habit. They have come to you with a demand, in unison, that you rule for one of them, so that the other may finally be at peace. You see in their faces that each would much rather lose.

effects.log: You rule for both, and for neither. They are both relieved, and go out, arm in arm, and are not seen for a day. In the evening they return with a jar of plum syrup.
They tell you. It takes an hour, and it is a small story, and sad. At the end they look at each other, and nod, and the quarrel is over.

events.text: The Shadow Lodge Kin of {b3_kin} meet in the cellar of an inn, among barrels, under a lamp that has been dimmed on purpose. You are given a low stool and a cup of something smoky. The Lodge Master, a woman with a face like a closed purse, asks you three questions. The first is: 'What do you know that no one has asked?'

effects.log: You answer. She writes nothing. Later you learn that what you said was exactly what she wanted to hear, and also exactly what she would have said herself.
She smiles, a thin small smile. 'A good answer,' she says. 'A very good one.' You are given a second cup.

events.text: In {b3_kin} nobody uses a real name. You are called Wick, because you have a habit of listening with your head tilted. The Lodge Master calls everyone by a household object. Your neighbour at the table is Ladle. The man across is Hearth. It is oddly intimate. You find you can say things as Wick that you could not as yourself.

effects.log: You say a thing you have never said aloud, and the table listens. Ladle passes you the bread. It is the first time in years someone has simply taken your confession as ordinary.
You say only what Wick would say. The Lodge notices, and says nothing. A slow, careful trust grows, in the manner of a long-kept plant.

events.text: {b3_kin} runs on debts: a favour given is a coin in the Lodge's jar. You have been given a favour, a small one, by a quiet man: he has moved a barrel for you. The barrel was heavy. He wants nothing now, and he will, one day, want something. He nods to you from across the room, and raises his cup.

effects.log: You send a loaf and a note. The man is faintly disappointed. 'You'll spoil the system,' he says. But he eats the loaf, and the favour stays on the books.
You let it ride. A year later, he calls it in, and the favour is large, and strange, and you do it, and he says it was worth the wait. The Lodge nods its approval.

events.text: A pupil from {b3_order} stumbles into the Lodge of {b3_kin} by mistake, lost and dizzy, and sits at your table. They do not know what the Lodge is. They are friendly, and they sing. The Lodge Master looks at you. Strangers who stumble in are normally walked out, quietly. The look says: your guest, your call.

effects.log: You walk them home through the dark streets. They sing the whole way. At the school gate they hug you, and are sick on your shoe. The Lodge, when you return, says nothing, and approves.
The Lodge sends them home with a blanket, a bun and no memory. You are uneasy. In the morning you feel better, and not entirely good.

events.text: The members of {b3_kin} sit round a stove, in the back of a salt warehouse, and eat. It is a quiet, strange, tender supper. Nobody asks what anyone does. Someone reads aloud from a seed catalogue. There is a cat. You are sitting beside an elderly man who is not called anything, and who seems to be the whole Lodge's grandfather.

effects.log: You ask what the Lodge is for. 'To remember who owes what,' he says. 'Nothing else.' He pats your hand, a papery pat, and goes back to the seeds.
You sit. The seeds are read, one by one. He falls asleep against your shoulder. The Lodge shifts quietly round, so as not to wake him.

events.text: The Lodge Master of {b3_kin} assigns you a task: follow a certain tax collector for a day and write down everything he eats. It is a joke, or a test, or a courtesy. The tax collector, a large mild man, spends the day eating small cakes, and talking to every dog. At evening he turns, and smiles. 'Hello,' he says. 'Have you eaten?'

effects.log: You say you were following him. He nods, and buys you a cake. You write down: 'He is kind to dogs.' The Lodge Master reads it and says, 'That is useful.'
He believes you, or does not mind. He gives you a cake. You write down all of it, anyway, and the report is, the Lodge Master says, the most thorough she has seen.

events.text: The first day at {b3_acad} you are given a slate, a stub of chalk and a seat by the window. The master, a thin patient woman with ink on her chin, writes a single word on the board: 'Why.' She sets the chalk down and asks the class to write what they think it means. You write nothing for a very long time.

effects.log: You write 'because.' She reads it, and smiles. 'That is the answer to every why,' she says. 'It is also the start of all of them.' You are placed in the second row.
You write 'Why not?' The master laughs, delighted, and keeps the slate. She says no one has ever answered the board with a question. You are placed in the front.

events.text: At {b3_acad} you share a desk with a fisherman's son who smells of the sea and cannot read. He listens to every lesson as if it were a song. At the end of the week the master sets a test, and the fisherman's son is called to the front. He recites the lesson, word for word, from memory, with enormous solemnity. The master has gone quiet.

effects.log: You teach him the alphabet, at night, with a candle stub. By spring he reads. He weeps over his first letter home, and you never forget his face.

choices.text: Ask the master to listen to him

effects.log: The master does. She decides that the boy shall be taught by ear, and he becomes the academy's most brilliant student of poems.

events.text: The students of {b3_acad} are marched, once a year, to the temple on the hill, to give thanks to the Maker. It is a long and boring walk. The priest at the top gives a sermon about gratitude, which lasts an hour, and everyone is bored, and then the priest says, quite simply, 'Thank you for coming,' and sits down. The silence is enormous.

choices.text: Say a prayer of your own

effects.log: You murmur one. It is short, and no one hears, and a warm, quiet feeling lies on your shoulder like a hand. You walk back down the hill lighter than you climbed.
You eat your lunch on the temple steps, and share a rice-cake with a stray dog. The dog is grateful, and so, in the end, is something larger.

events.text: The headmaster of {b3_acad} is known for punishing lateness with a single question: 'What was more important than being here?' This morning you are late, because you stopped to help an old woman with a cart. You enter the room, red-faced. The headmaster looks at you over his spectacles and asks the question.

effects.log: You tell him. He nods slowly, and says, 'Then you were not late. You were elsewhere.' He waves you to your seat. The whole class stares. You are not punished.
You say you overslept. He sighs, and gives you a line to copy a hundred times. The line is: 'I will not be late.' Your hand cramps. The old woman's cart, you hope, made it up the hill.

events.text: A rich student at {b3_acad} has been paying other pupils to do his sums. You are offered a coin. The sum is easy. The coin is real, and money is short at home, and the student is polite about it. He looks at you with a faint, hopeful, entitled smile. The master, at the front, is not looking.

choices.text: Take the coin and do the sum

effects.log: You do the sum. The coin buys a month of lamp oil for the house. The guilt lasts longer than the oil.

choices.text: Refuse and offer to teach him

effects.log: You refuse and offer to teach him. He is astonished, then sullen, then intrigued. In a year he can do his own sums, and he gives you, of his own accord, a coin and a thank-you.

events.text: The last day of term at {b3_acad} is a holiday of sorts. The master brings in a sack of apples and the students eat them in the yard. A girl in the corner is not eating hers. She is crying, quietly, into the apple. She has to leave the academy: her family can no longer pay. Nobody else has noticed.

effects.log: You sit with her, and say nothing, and share the apple. The master, passing, says: 'Come and see me.' In a month, a scholarship appears. She never knows who asked.
You tell the master. She listens, nods, and says: 'I know. I have been trying to find a way.' She finds one, in a week. The girl stays.

events.text: Your final examination at {b3_acad} is to teach a lesson to a class of the youngest children, on any subject you choose. You have chosen the stars. The children sit cross-legged, with enormous eyes. A boy at the front asks, loudly, 'Is the moon a lamp?' Behind you the examiners lean forward with pens.

choices.text: Say yes, it is a lamp

effects.log: You say it is a lamp lit by the Maker, and the children gasp. The examiners wince. The boy beams. You pass with a note: 'Poetic. Inaccurate. Admirable.'
You say nobody is sure. The children look at each other. A girl says: 'Then we can find out.' The examiners, one by one, put down their pens. You pass with distinction.

events.text: On the evening of graduation from {b3_acad} each pupil is given a lantern, lit, to carry home through the town. The streets are full of children with lanterns, strung out like a slow river. You find yourself walking beside a boy from the first year who is carrying yours, because you have dropped it. He is trying very hard not to spill the oil.

effects.log: He carries it all the way to your door. You thank him with a coin and a cake. He walks home alone in the dark, the proudest child in the town.
You each hold one side of the handle. It is a little awkward, a little slow. The two of you walk through the lights without speaking, and it is the best part of the night.

events.text: Young Heroes' Day opens with a parade down the main street, led by a band of boys with drums, and followed by every school in the kingdom, each under its own banner. {b3_order}'s banner is old, faded, a pale green. The crowd cheers anyway. Your pupil, at the end of the line, is waving with both arms.

effects.log: You wave. Your pupil sees, and almost drops the banner. They march with a straighter back for the rest of the day, and win nothing, and it does not matter.

choices.text: Buy them a sweet from the stall

effects.log: You press a sticky bun into their hand at the first corner. They eat it on the march, grinning, and the banner leans.

events.text: In the great bout at Young Heroes' Day your pupil faces a boy of the neighbouring kingdom, tall, polite, with a stutter. The crowd roars. The stutterer bows and cannot say his name. Your pupil, who has a stutter of their own on bad days, bows back, and says it for him. The referee, at a loss, calls it for love.

effects.log: You applaud so loudly the referee notices. The match is declared a draw, and the two are given a joint medal, and a plate of dumplings to share. They become friends for life.
You keep quiet, and let it be theirs. After, they find you in the crowd and stand beside you, silent, with the medal. You say nothing, and everything.

events.text: At Young Heroes' Day, the boys' wrestling is held in a ring of sawdust under an awning. Your pupil is small and fierce. Her opponent is twice her size and genial. She loses in seconds, picked up like a sack. She comes out of the ring spitting sawdust and laughing, and says: 'Again!' The big boy blushes.

effects.log: She goes again. And again. By the fifth, she has learned how to fall. The crowd, charmed, cheers every one. She is awarded a ribbon for Spirit, and the big boy is made to carry it.

choices.text: Teach her a trick between rounds

effects.log: You show her a simple trip. On the sixth round she uses it. The big boy sits down with astonishment. The crowd howls. A new legend begins.

events.text: A small hawker sells fried dough outside the arena at Young Heroes' Day, and your pupil has run out of coins. The hawker, a thin elderly man, waves away the coins. 'First one is free for the school with the green banner,' he says. 'I used to wear it.' Your pupil looks at you. You look at the old man. He has the school's old badge pinned inside his coat.

choices.text: Thank him and sit with him

effects.log: You buy two and sit with him on the kerb. He tells you about his year. It was fifty years ago. He remembers every bout. Your pupil listens with a wide-open face.

choices.text: Ask the head to invite him to the feast

effects.log: You send a message. That evening the old man sits at the head table, in his badge, beside your pupil. He cries once, quietly, into the soup, and no one says anything.

events.text: The final of Young Heroes' Day is a race up a hill with an egg on a spoon. It is a hundred years old and has no use. Your pupil is neck and neck with a girl from the hills, who runs with the spoon in her teeth. The crowd is screaming. At the summit a priest waits with a ribbon. Your pupil's egg wobbles and drops.

effects.log: You cheer so loudly the hill rings. The egg rolls down, unbroken, and a goat eats it. Your pupil laughs till they cannot stand. The girl from the hills wins, and shares the ribbon.

choices.text: Run up the hill to meet them

effects.log: You run, panting, and arrive as they sit down on the grass at the top, shaking with laughter. You sit beside them. The hill is very green, and the sky enormous.

events.text: The Road Wardens of {b3_side} meet at a crossroads inn in the dead of the afternoon, when the roads are quiet. A Warden-Captain with a broken nose passes you a map covered in small, tidy marks. 'These are the places where the road bites,' she says. 'Walk them. Tell me what you see.' You take the map and a loaf.

effects.log: You walk it for a season. You find a bridge missing a plank, a tavern that waters its beer, a family that lives under a cart. You report all of it. The Captain nods. 'Good eyes,' she says.
You walk the worst places and, in a ditch, find a lost traveller half-frozen. You carry her to a farm. The Captain, told, says nothing, and takes your loaf.

events.text: A ford on the river has been claimed by a local lord, who charges a toll and builds nothing. The Wardens of {b3_side} have been told to remind him, politely, whose road it is. The lord is a plump, red man in embroidered slippers who is delighted to see you, and offers a seat. His ford is shallow and steady and very well kept.

effects.log: You cite the old charters, and the lord, who has never read them, goes pale. He agrees to let the toll go in exchange for a rule that the ford be kept. It is, in the end, a better ford.
You admire the ford sincerely. The lord, touched, lets the toll fall by half and invites you to dinner. The ford is better kept, and the road is a little freer.

events.text: A bandit leader has been caught by the Wardens of {b3_side}, a young woman of twenty with a hat full of feathers. She has been robbing travelling merchants, and returning half the goods to the poor. She sits in the lock-up, cheerful. The Warden-Captain looks to you: do we hang her, or release her?

effects.log: You argue for release, with conditions. She is let go, on the promise that she will guard the road she once robbed. She does, for forty years, in a hat full of feathers, and is the best Warden of her generation.
You hold her. The magistrate, a tired man, gives her a year of road-mending. She mends it well. She never forgives you, nor entirely blames you.

events.text: The Wardens of {b3_side} have a custom: when a Warden dies, the others walk the road they walked, in a line, ringing a small bell. The walk is long and quiet. Today it is an old man named Hobb, whom everyone loved, who died in his bed. You are asked to carry the bell at the front. It is very small. It weighs nothing at all.

effects.log: You carry it for twelve miles. Each village, as you pass, turns out to bow. At the last bridge you ring it three times, and a kingfisher darts across the water.

choices.text: Ask to carry the bell with someone else

effects.log: A young Warden, red-eyed, takes the other side of the strap. You walk together, in step, the whole way. It is the most honest friendship the road has ever made.

events.text: A flood has taken a village off the map, and the Wardens of {b3_side} are sent to mark the new edges of the river. They work for a week with stakes and string. At the end you stand on a hill and look at the shining water. A child's shoe floats by. Somebody has to say something. They look at you.

choices.text: Say a prayer to the Maker

effects.log: You say it aloud. The Wardens, in a rough ring, bow their heads. The river, for a moment, is perfectly still. Then it moves, and they move, and the road goes on.
You wade in and rescue the shoe. It goes on a stake at the new edge, a little mark. When the child, older, comes back, she finds it, and weeps, and puts it on.

events.text: The Shadow Lodges of {b3_side} keep their books in a chandler's shop, in a back room that smells of tallow. The chandler is a cheerful woman who sells candles and quietly records every price in the district. She hands you a ledger and says: 'Read me the price of salt in the three towns you have lived in.' You do, from memory.

effects.log: You give the true prices. She writes them down, nods, and says: 'You'll do.' The Lodges run on exactly this: what everything costs, honestly kept.

choices.text: Give the prices as they ought to be

effects.log: You give the prices you think are fair. She laughs, and writes them down in red. 'Now we know what you want the world to be,' she says. It is no less useful.

events.text: A Lodge Hand brings you a packet in the dark, from a dyer's yard, and tells you not to open it. It is warm, and smells of lemon. You are to carry it to a house in the next street and leave it on the step. A watchman walks the street. He looks at the packet in your hands, and at your face, and slowly turns his back.

effects.log: You leave it on the step. A window opens, an old hand reaches out, and the packet is gone. The watchman, still turned, coughs. In the morning a bun is left at your door.
It is a lemon cake, in a cloth. You eat a crumb, and wrap it again. The Lodge, later, says nothing, but you are given a cake the next week, a bigger one.

events.text: The Lodges of {b3_side} are said to know the price of everything, and they will tell you, for a fee. A young man comes to your door asking the price of forgiveness. He has wronged a brother. He has money. You are, as the Lodge's representative, expected to name a figure. He holds out a purse.

choices.text: Tell him it cannot be bought

effects.log: You push the purse back, gently. 'It costs one visit,' you say, 'and the first sentence.' He goes pale and nods. A month later, a letter arrives: it worked.
You name a coin, to be paid to the poor. He pays, and goes. You do not know what became of him. You hope the coin helped, and the forgiveness more.

events.text: A smuggler of the Lodges of {b3_side} is brought in, bruised, from a failed run, and put to bed in the loft above a bakery. She has a broken arm and a joke for everyone. You are asked to sit with her through the night. She will not take any tea, but says: 'Tell me what you would be if you weren't this.'

effects.log: You tell her: a gardener, or a teacher. She nods, and says she would have been a singer. She sings, half asleep, a low song about the sea. You stay, listening, till dawn.
You say you would be a goat. She laughs so hard she cries. It is the best night of her convalescence, and you are called 'Goat' by the entire Lodge for years.

events.text: The Lodges of {b3_side} are asked by a village to find out who is selling short measure at the market. Everyone suspects the butcher, who is huge and loud. You follow the scales for a week. The short measure, you find, is in the baker's weights, which are bent with age. He is a gentle widower with five children. He has never noticed.

effects.log: You tell him, in the back of his shop, with a new set of weights. He weeps, and thanks you, and sells at fair measure from that day. The village never knows.
You report it to the market warden. The baker is fined, and shamed, and the butcher is exonerated and unbearable. You are not proud of the result.

events.text: The morning drill at {b3_order} starts, as it has for two hundred years, with everyone facing the east and holding their breath for a count of nine. It is meant to be a moment of attention. Today a swallow lands on the head of the pupil in front of you, and stays. Nobody dares breathe, in case it flies away.

choices.text: Hold your breath for the swallow

effects.log: You hold it, and so does the whole line. The swallow, aware of the stillness, takes its time. When it leaves, everyone exhales at once, and the yard shakes with laughter.
You breathe out. The swallow leaves in a small startled arc. The pupil in front turns, frowning, then laughing. 'It was the best thing to happen to my hair all year,' they say.

events.text: In the kitchen of {b3_order} there is a pot that has been simmering since before anyone was born. It is a stew, and nobody knows what is in it. Each cook adds something, a bone, a carrot, a secret. Today the cook beckons you over, with a spoon, and says: 'Taste, and tell me what it needs.'

effects.log: You taste, and think, and say: 'Salt.' The cook looks astonished. 'Three hundred years,' she says, 'and no one has said salt.' She adds some. It is, then, perfect.

choices.text: Taste and say it needs nothing

effects.log: You say it needs nothing. The cook beams. 'Honest,' she says. She gives you a bowl, and the pot goes on, as it has, simmering the same.

events.text: The school {b3_order} has a tradition of the Winter Letter: each pupil writes a letter to themselves, to be read in the spring. The letters are sealed in clay jars and buried. Yours says only: 'Be kind to the one who is writing this.' When you read it in spring, you do not remember writing it, and are, for a moment, very moved.

effects.log: You write another. It says: 'You did it.' You bury it with care. In spring you will dig it up, and it will be true.

choices.text: Keep the old one in your pocket

effects.log: You keep the letter, soft with handling. When things are bad, you take it out. 'Be kind,' it says. You are, a little.

events.text: {b3_order}'s well freezes in the deepest cold, and for a week the pupils have to melt snow for tea. The water tastes of smoke and iron. The younger ones complain, the older ones remember worse. On the sixth night, an old cook sings a song in the kitchen, and the whole school, in blankets, comes to listen.

effects.log: You join. It is a plain, sad, happy song about a river in summer. The old cook cries, and the pupils sing louder. By morning, the well has thawed, and they say it was the song.
You stir a giant pot of soup, with onions, and a few coins' worth of dried beans. You feed seventy. The cook says it is the finest soup of the winter, and she does not usually say that.

events.text: A visitor comes to {b3_order}, a travelling storyteller with a drum on her back and a limp. She asks for a night's shelter and offers a story in exchange. The head hesitates. The pupils, hearing, gather at the door. Her story is about a girl who tried to catch the moon with a bucket. It lasts an hour, and nobody moves.

effects.log: She stays a month. She tells a new story each night. The school is never quite the same, and neither, she says, is she. When she leaves she gives each pupil a word to keep.

choices.text: Give her a pack of food and your thanks

effects.log: You press food and a coin into her hands. She kisses your cheek, and limps on. You hear her drum, receding on the road, for a long time.

events.text: {b3_order} is given, by a grateful village, a bell. It is a good bell, with a deep voice. The trouble is that it is cracked, and rings two notes at once. The head wants to hang it anyway. The pupils like it. The neighbours complain. The bell, in the yard, waiting, gives a small questioning clank, as if asking.

effects.log: You hang it over the gate. It rings, at dawn, in two notes at once, and it is the strangest, loveliest sound in the district. The neighbours, in a year, would not be without it.
You find a smith who can fix a crack. It takes months. The bell, mended, rings one note. It is purer, and flatter, and the school misses the double voice.

events.text: The cat of {b3_order}, a one-eyed grey creature of enormous dignity, has been missing for three days. The pupils are frantic. They have searched the cellar, the stables and the hayloft. A child finds it, on the fourth day, in the head's bed, fast asleep, and refuses to move the animal. The head, found in the hall, is asleep on a bench.

effects.log: You leave them. The cat wakes at dusk, stretches, and stalks out as if nothing had happened. The head wakes, embarrassed, and finds a tuna on the table, which is a sort of apology.
You wake the head gently with tea. They sigh. 'I have been so tired,' they say. They sleep, afterwards, nine hours, and are better for it.

events.text: The school {b3_order} has a ritual: on the last night of the year, everyone writes a regret on a slip of paper and drops it in the fire. The fire burns blue for a moment each time. You have written yours. It is a small one, and it has been a long time. You hold the slip, and look at the flames. A pupil beside you, who is eight, asks what it says.

effects.log: You tell her. She nods, solemn, and says, 'That's a good regret.' You drop it in the fire, and it burns a beautiful, clear blue.
You say it is a secret. She nods, and writes hers, and shows you: it says 'I broke the pot.' You say it is a very good regret, and you both watch it burn.

events.text: At the spring festival of {b3_order}, the pupils are paired for a dance, which is a form of the school's oldest drill done to a fiddle. You are paired with the oldest pupil in the school, a gnarled man of ninety who takes it terribly seriously. He bows. He holds out a hand like a root. The fiddler begins. Everyone is watching.

effects.log: You dance it properly, as slowly as he needs. He is a marvel. The crowd falls silent, and then cheers. At the end he whispers: 'I have waited forty years for a partner who could keep time.'
You dance it badly. He roars with laughter. The two of you lurch round the floor, to the thunder of the fiddle. The school will remember the old man's laugh for years.

events.text: A letter comes for {b3_order} from the king's own scribe, in a thick cream envelope, and the whole school gathers to hear it opened. It says: 'In recognition of your service, the school is awarded one sack of rice and a good word.' The rice is delivered by an embarrassed boy with a barrow. The good word, he says, is 'adequate.' The head reads it aloud, twice.

effects.log: You frame it. It hangs in the hall, above the stove. The school, in time, grows rather fond of the word 'adequate'. It becomes a high compliment.
You eat the rice. It is excellent. The school feasts for a week on the king's adequate good word, and sends back a thank-you in a very elaborate hand.
